tasks.entryName: Riesz representation theorem for Hilbert spaces
tasks.entryDescription: Orthogonal projection onto kernel; minimization of distance; polarization and representing vector.
tasks.currentSketch: For a nonzero bounded functional f on a Hilbert space, ker(f) is a closed subspace and its orthogonal complement is one-dimensional. Choose nonzero x₀ in ker(f)⊥ and set z_f=f(x₀)x₀/||x₀||² (adjusting conjugation for the inner-product convention). On ker(f), both f and ⟨z_f,·⟩ vanish; on ker(f)⊥, which is spanned by x₀, they agree by construction. Hence f(x)=⟨z_f,x⟩ for all x.

tasks.currentSketch: Minimize distance from a point x with ℓ(x)=1 to the closed subspace kerℓ. Projection theorem gives u=x−proj(x) perpendicular to kerℓ; for any y, y−(ℓ(y))x∈kerℓ, so ℓ(y)=⟨y,u⟩/⟨x,u⟩, with convention-adjusted conjugation.

tasks.currentSketch: Let M=kerℓ and choose unit u spanning M⊥. Decompose x=m+αu; linearity forces ℓ(x)=αℓ(u), so choose v with ⟨x,v⟩=ℓ(x). Polarization can recover inner products from norm data, but by itself does not construct v; this route needs Riesz/projection machinery.

tasks.entryName: Open mapping theorem for Banach spaces
tasks.entryDescription: Baire category and nested balls; quotient-space argument; closed graph theorem followed by inverse mapping.
tasks.currentSketch: It suffices to show T(B_X(0,1)) contains a neighborhood of 0. Surjectivity gives Y=⋃_n T(B_X(0,n)); Baire implies the closure of one such image has interior. By linearity and subtraction this yields a ball around 0 contained in the closure of T(B_X(0,1)). Repeatedly approximate a target y by T(x₁), then its residual by T(x₂), with ||x_k|| geometrically decreasing. The sum converges in X and maps to y, so a neighborhood of 0 lies in T(B_X(0,1)); scaling and translation show T is open.

tasks.currentSketch: Factor T through ker T: the induced map X/kerT→Y is bounded bijective between Banach spaces. Prove its inverse bounded via Baire/open mapping; hence T maps open sets to open sets. This route relies on the quotient Banach property and open mapping core.

tasks.routeTitle: closed graph theorem followed by inverse mapping
tasks.currentSketch: Apply closed graph theorem to the inverse of a bounded bijection T; its graph is closed, so inverse is bounded. For a surjective T, pass to quotient by kerT first. This is an equivalent theorem network, not a proof independent of closed graph/open mapping.

tasks.entryDescription: Open mapping theorem on the graph; Baire category directly; uniform boundedness plus duality.
tasks.routeTitle: Open mapping theorem on the graph
tasks.currentSketch: The graph G(T) is a closed subspace of Banach X×Y, hence Banach. Projection P:G→X is a bounded bijection; open mapping makes P^{-1} bounded. Then T=Q∘P^{-1} is bounded.

tasks.currentSketch: If T's graph is closed but T were unbounded, choose x_n with ||x_n||≤2^{-n} and ||Tx_n||≥n. Baire-category/open-set arguments construct a convergent series x with images violating closedness/continuity. Standard direct proofs often recast this argument through Baire; full details require bounded-domain construction.

tasks.entryDescription: Contraction mapping/fixed point; Newton iteration with estimates; differential/topological degree.
tasks.currentSketch: Normalize F(x)=0, DF(0)=I. On a small ball, G_y(x)=x−F(x)+y is a contraction because DF is close to I. For small y it maps the ball to itself; the fixed point solves F(x)=y, giving local inverse; derivative estimates yield C¹ inverse.

tasks.entryDescription: Contraction mapping/fixed point; Newton iteration with estimates; differential/topological degree.
tasks.currentSketch: Newton iteration x_{n+1}=x_n−DF(x_n)^{-1}(F(x_n)−y) is a contraction under a uniform inverse bound and Lipschitz derivative. The convergence estimates give a unique root near the base point and smooth dependence. This is quantitative contraction proof; hypotheses require C¹ plus local derivative control.

tasks.entryDescription: Contraction mapping/fixed point; Newton iteration with estimates; differential/topological degree.
tasks.currentSketch: Degree theory proves local solvability: on a small boundary F stays away from nearby target values, and local degree equals sign det DF(a)≠0; homotopy invariance forces each nearby target to have a preimage. This proves local onto, while injectivity follows derivative closeness; degree alone needs those local controls.

tasks.currentSketch: For F(x,y)=0 with D_yF invertible, apply the inverse function theorem to (x,y)↦(x,F(x,y)); local inverse yields y=g(x) and differentiating gives Dg=−(D_yF)^{-1}D_xF.

tasks.entryDescription: Inverse function theorem; contraction mapping in solved variables; local coordinate/submersion theorem.
tasks.currentSketch: Rewrite y=y−A F(x,y), where A=(D_yF(a,b))^{-1}. On a small y-ball this is a contraction uniformly for x near a and maps the ball into itself. Its unique fixed point gives g(x); parameter dependence gives differentiability.

tasks.currentSketch: View F^{-1}(0) near a regular point as a level submanifold by the submersion theorem; projection to x-coordinates has invertible tangent map, so is a local coordinate chart and the zero set is a graph. This route invokes the submersion theorem, usually proved from IFT.

tasks.routeTitle: Differential forms and local charts/partition of unity
tasks.currentSketch: In Euclidean space, prove Stokes on a coordinate box by integrating each coefficient of dω in its coordinate direction and applying the one-variable fundamental theorem; interior faces cancel and only the oriented boundary terms remain. A partition of unity reduces a compactly supported form on a manifold to these local box calculations, which add to ∫ₘdω=∫∂ₘω.

tasks.routeTitle: reduce to the fundamental theorem of calculus on boxes
tasks.currentSketch: Write a compactly supported (n−1)-form on a rectangle as a sum of terms omitting one coordinate differential. Its exterior derivative contributes the corresponding partial derivative. Integrating each partial derivative over the box and using the one-variable fundamental theorem gives the integral over the two opposite faces; summing over coordinates produces the oriented boundary integral.

tasks.currentSketch: Triangulate an oriented manifold into compatible simplices and integrate a differential form simplex by simplex. On each simplex, the simplex Stokes formula identifies the integral of dω with the integral over its oriented faces. Every interior face occurs twice with opposite orientations and cancels, leaving exactly the boundary simplices, hence ∫ₘdω=∫∂ₘω.
